summary: Describes how an IPv4 host can configure an address for itself automatically when no DHCP server or manual setup is available. The host picks an address from a reserved link-local range and checks that nobody else on the link uses it, which gives a usable subset of networking on a local link.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3927 describes how a computer can give itself an IP address when no one else will. It picks a random address from the 169.254.0.0 range, which is reserved for local use, and then checks that nobody else has picked the same one.

The check is done with ARP, the protocol that maps addresses to hardware addresses on a local network. The computer broadcasts a probe asking whether the address is free, waits, and if it hears anything back it picks another address and tries again.

questions: automatic ip address configuration without dhcp
how does ipv4 link-local autoconfiguration work
subtitle: How a host picks itself an address on the local link when no server gives it one.

tldr.problem: A host normally gets its IP address from a DHCP server or from an administrator. When neither is available, for example on an ad hoc wireless network, the host has no address at all and cannot use familiar tools such as FTP for local communication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3927 lets a host choose an address from the 169.254/16 prefix at random, then claim it by broadcasting ARP probes and listening for a reply. If someone else is using the address the host picks a new one, and it keeps watching for conflicts for as long as it holds the address.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from May 2005 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It also spells out the cost: a Link-Local address only works on its own link, it changes without warning, and the ARP protocol underneath it is not secure.

today: RFC 3927 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2005. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of IPv4 link-local address autoconfiguration and the rules that hosts and routers follow when a link-local address is in use.

sections.title: Introduction and Applicability
sections.content:
As the Internet Protocol continues to grow in popularity, it becomes increasingly valuable to be able to use familiar IP tools such as FTP not only for global communication, but for local communication as well. Two people with laptop computers supporting IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs may meet and wish to exchange files, and it is desirable for them to be able to use IP application software without the inconvenience of having to configure static IP addresses manually or set up a DHCP server.

The document describes a method by which a host may automatically configure an interface with an IPv4 address in the 169.254/16 prefix that is valid for link-local communication on that interface. This is especially valuable in environments where no other configuration mechanism is available. The prefix 169.254/16 is registered with the IANA for this purpose. Allocation of IPv6 link-local addresses is described in RFC 2462.

Link-local communication using IPv4 link-local addresses is only suitable for communication with other devices connected to the same physical or logical link, and is not suitable for communication with devices not directly connected to that link. Microsoft Windows 98 and later and Mac OS 8.5 and later already support this capability; the document standardizes usage, prescribing rules for how link-local addresses are to be treated by hosts and routers, including how routers behave when receiving packets with link-local addresses in the source or destination address.

A set of hosts is considered to be on the same link if, when any host in the set sends a packet to any other host in the set using unicast, multicast or broadcast, the entire link-layer packet payload arrives unmodified, and if a broadcast sent over that link by any host in the set can be received by every other host in the set. The link-layer header may be modified, but not the payload. A packet may therefore pass through repeaters, bridges, hubs or switches and still be on the same link, but not through an IP router that decrements the TTL or otherwise modifies the IP header.

The specification applies to all IEEE 802 LANs, including Ethernet, Token Ring and IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, as well as to other link-layer technologies that operate at data rates of at least 1 Mbps, have a round-trip latency of at most one second, and support ARP. Link-layer technologies outside those bounds may need different values for the probe and announcement parameters, the maximum rate at which address claiming may be attempted, and the interval below which a host must reconfigure instead of defending its address.

The specification is intended for use with small ad hoc networks, a single link containing only a few hosts. Although 65024 link-local addresses are available in principle, attempting to use all of them on a single link would give a high probability of conflicts. Operators with more than 1300 hosts on a single link may want to consider dividing that link into two or more subnets. A host joining a link that already has 1300 hosts has a 98% chance of selecting an unused address on the first try and a 99.96% chance within two tries; the probability of needing more than ten tries is about 1 in 10^17.
sections.plainLanguage:
The idea is simple: every host on a small network picks its own address at random, and the rules make sure that two hosts do not end up with the same one.

The address only means anything on the wire it is chosen on. A router that decrements the time-to-live ends the link, so a host with only a link-local address cannot reach anything past the router.

sections.title: Where Link-Local Addresses May and May Not Be Used
sections.content:
IPv4 link-local addresses and their dynamic configuration have profound implications for applications. Many applications fundamentally assume that the addresses of communicating peers are routable, relatively unchanging and unique. Those assumptions no longer hold with link-local addresses, or with a mixture of link-local and routable IPv4 addresses. Some applications will work properly, others will do so only after modification, and others will exhibit reduced or partial functionality. In some cases it may be infeasible to modify the application.

Link-local addresses should therefore only be used where stable, routable addresses are not available, such as on ad hoc or isolated networks, or in controlled situations where the limitations are understood and accepted. The document does not recommend that link-local and routable addresses be configured simultaneously on the same interface. Use of link-local addresses in off-link communication is likely to cause application failures, and this can occur in any application that includes embedded addresses. Examples include IPsec, Kerberos 4 and 5, FTP, RSVP, SMTP, SIP, X-Windows, Xterm, Telnet, Real Audio, H.323 and SNMP.

To preclude the use of link-local addresses in off-link communication, the document advises that link-local addresses must not be configured in the DNS. DNS clients must not send queries for any name that falls within the 254.169.in-addr.arpa domain, and recursive name servers receiving such queries from non-compliant clients must by default return RCODE 3, authoritatively asserting that no such name exists. Names that are globally resolvable to routable addresses should be used within applications whenever they are available; names resolvable only on the local link must not be used in off-link communication, and addresses and names that can only be resolved on the local link should not be forwarded beyond the local link. If names resolvable to globally routable addresses are not available but the globally routable addresses are, the routable addresses should be used instead.

Addresses in the 169.254/16 prefix should not be configured manually or by a DHCP server, because such configuration may cause a host to use an address without following the special rules regarding duplicate detection and automatic configuration that pertain to this prefix. While the DHCP specification indicates that a client should probe a newly received address with ARP, this is not mandatory, and even a server that probes with an ICMP Echo Request cannot detect a conflict, because link-local addresses are not routable and a server not directly connected to a link cannot see the hosts on it. Administrators wishing to configure their own local addresses should use one of the existing private address prefixes instead.

A host with an operable routable address available on an interface should not also assign a link-local address on that interface. During the transition in either direction between routable and link-local addresses, both may be in use at once subject to three rules. The assignment of a link-local address is based solely on the state of the interface and is independent of any other protocol such as DHCP, and a host must not alter its behaviour or use of DHCP because it has assigned a link-local address. If an interface that previously had a link-local address now has an operable routable address, the host must use the routable address for new communications and must stop advertising the availability of the link-local address, though it should continue to use the link-local address for communications already underway and may continue to accept new communications addressed to it. If an interface no longer has an operable routable address, the host may identify a usable link-local address and assign it to the interface.
sections.plainLanguage:
The address is useful and dangerous at the same time. It works on the local wire and nowhere else, so an application that writes the address into a message for someone on another network will fail.

For that reason link-local addresses must never go into the DNS, and they should not be handed out by a DHCP server, because a server cannot check whether an address is already in use on a link it is not attached to.

sections.title: Choosing a Link-Local Address
sections.content:
When a host wishes to configure an IPv4 link-local address, it selects an address using a pseudo-random number generator with a uniform distribution in the range from 169.254.1.0 to 169.254.254.255 inclusive. The prefix 169.254/16 is registered with the IANA for this purpose. The first 256 and last 256 addresses in that prefix are reserved for future use and must not be selected by a host using this dynamic configuration mechanism.

The pseudo-random number generation algorithm must be chosen so that different hosts do not generate the same sequence of numbers. If the host has access to persistent information that is different for each host, such as its IEEE 802 MAC address, the generator should be seeded using a value derived from that information. This means that even without any other persistent storage, a host will usually select the same link-local address each time it is booted, which is convenient for debugging and other operational reasons. Seeding the generator using the real-time clock, or any other information which is or may be identical in every host, is not suitable, because a group of hosts powered on at the same time might all generate the same sequence, resulting in a never-ending series of conflicts as the hosts move in lock-step through exactly the same sequence and conflict on every address they probe.

Hosts equipped with persistent storage may, for each interface, record the IPv4 address they selected. On booting, hosts with a previously recorded address should use that address as their first candidate when probing. This increases the stability of addresses. If a group of hosts are powered off at night and then powered on the next morning, they will all resume using the same addresses instead of picking different ones and potentially having to resolve conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage:
The address is picked at random from the middle of the reserved range, with the first and last 256 addresses left aside.

The random number generator must be seeded differently on each host, ideally from the network hardware address, so that two machines that switch on at the same moment do not walk through the same list of candidates together and collide on every one.

sections.title: Claiming the Address with ARP Probes
sections.content:
After it has selected an address, a host must test whether the address is already in use before beginning to use it. When a network interface transitions from an inactive to an active state, the host does not know what link-local addresses may currently be in use on that link, since the point of attachment may have changed or the interface may have been inactive when a conflicting address was claimed. Were the host to immediately begin using an address that is already in use by another host, that would be disruptive to the other host. Since it is possible that the host has changed its point of attachment, a routable address may be obtainable on the new network, and so it cannot be assumed that a link-local address is to be preferred.

Before using the address, either as the source address in an IPv4 packet or as the Sender IPv4 address in an ARP packet, the host must perform the probing test. Events that involve an interface becoming active include reboot or startup, waking from sleep if the interface was inactive during sleep, bringing up a previously inactive interface, a hardware link-state change, and association with a wireless base station or ad hoc network. A host must not perform this check periodically as a matter of course, because it would waste network bandwidth and is unnecessary given the ability to discover conflicts passively.

On a link-layer that supports ARP, conflict detection is done using ARP probes. A host probes to see if an address is already in use by broadcasting an ARP Request for the desired address. The client must fill in the sender hardware address field with the hardware address of the interface through which it is sending the packet. The sender IP address field must be set to all zeroes, to avoid polluting ARP caches in other hosts on the link in the case where the address turns out to be in use by another host. The target hardware address field is ignored and should be set to all zeroes, and the target IP address field must be set to the address being probed. An ARP Request constructed this way with an all-zero sender IP address is called an ARP Probe.

When ready to begin probing, the host should wait for a random time interval selected uniformly in the range zero to PROBE_WAIT seconds, and should then send PROBE_NUM probe packets, each spaced randomly PROBE_MIN to PROBE_MAX seconds apart. If, from the beginning of the probing process until ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the last probe packet is sent, the host receives any ARP packet, request or reply, on the interface where the probe is being performed whose sender IP address is the address being probed for, then the host must treat the address as being in use by some other host, must select a new pseudo-random address, and repeat the process. If during this period the host receives any ARP Probe whose target IP address is the address being probed for and whose sender hardware address is not the hardware address of the interface the host is attempting to configure, the host must similarly treat this as an address conflict and select a new address. This can occur if two or more hosts attempt to configure the same address at the same time.

The host should maintain a counter of the number of address conflicts it has experienced in trying to acquire an address, and if the number of conflicts exceeds MAX_CONFLICTS the host must limit the rate at which it probes for new addresses to no more than one new address per RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL. This prevents catastrophic ARP storms in pathological failure cases, such as a rogue host that answers all ARP probes, causing legitimate hosts to go into an infinite loop attempting to select a usable address. If, by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the transmission of the last ARP Probe, no conflicting ARP Reply or ARP Probe has been received, the host has successfully claimed the desired address.
sections.plainLanguage:
Before using the address, the host asks the network whether anyone else has it. It waits a random moment first, so that a group of machines starting together do not all probe in lock-step, and it sends several probes spread over a couple of seconds.

If anything at all comes back mentioning that address, the address is taken and the whole process starts again with a new one. A host that keeps losing has to slow down, so that one broken machine answering every probe cannot flood the link.

sections.title: Announcing, Detecting and Defending an Address
sections.content:
Having probed to determine a unique address to use, the host must announce its claimed address by broadcasting ANNOUNCE_NUM ARP announcements, spaced ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL seconds apart. An ARP announcement is identical to the ARP Probe, except that now the sender and target IP addresses are both set to the host's newly selected IPv4 address. The purpose of these announcements is to make sure that other hosts on the link do not have stale ARP cache entries left over from some other host that may previously have been using the same address.

Address conflict detection is not limited to the address selection phase. It is an ongoing process that is in effect for as long as a host is using a link-local address. At any time, if a host receives an ARP packet, request or reply, on an interface where the sender IP address is the address the host has configured for that interface, but the sender hardware address does not match the hardware address of that interface, then this is a conflicting ARP packet indicating an address conflict.

A host must respond to a conflicting ARP packet in one of two ways. It may elect to immediately configure a new link-local address. Or, if it currently has active TCP connections or other reasons to prefer to keep the same address, and it has not seen any other conflicting ARP packets within the last DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, it may elect to attempt to defend its address by recording the time the conflicting packet was received and then broadcasting one single ARP announcement, giving its own IP and hardware addresses as the sender addresses of the ARP. Having done this, the host can continue to use the address normally. If this is not the first conflicting ARP packet the host has seen and the time recorded for the previous one is recent, within DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, then the host must immediately cease using this address and configure a new one, so that two hosts do not get stuck in an endless loop with both trying to defend the same address. A host must not ignore conflicting ARP packets.

Forced address reconfiguration may be disruptive, causing TCP connections to be broken, but such disruptions are expected to be rare, and if inadvertent address duplication happens then disruption of communication is inevitable, no matter how the addresses were assigned. It is not possible for two different hosts using the same IP address on the same network to operate reliably. Before abandoning an address due to a conflict, hosts should actively attempt to reset any existing connections using that address, which mitigates some of the security threats posed by address reconfiguration.

All ARP packets, replies as well as requests, that contain a link-local sender IP address must be sent using link-layer broadcast instead of link-layer unicast. This aids timely detection of duplicate addresses.
sections.plainLanguage:
Once the address is claimed, the host announces it so that other machines refresh their cache entries.

From then on the host keeps listening. If it hears an ARP packet claiming its address from different hardware, it has two choices: give up the address at once, or, if it has live connections and has not seen a conflict recently, send one announcement to say the address is still its own. Two hosts that keep defending the same address would lock each other out, so the second conflict within the defend interval forces a change.

sections.title: Forwarding Rules for Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
A host implementing this specification has additional rules to conform to, whether or not it has an interface configured with a link-local address. Since each interface may have a link-local address in addition to zero or more other addresses configured by other means, a host may have to make a choice about what source address to use when it sends a packet or initiates a TCP connection. Where both a link-local and a routable address are available on the same interface, the routable address should be preferred as the source address for new communications, but packets sent from or to the link-local address are still delivered as expected. The link-local address may continue to be used as a source address in communications where switching to a preferred address would cause failure because of the requirements of an upper-layer protocol, for example an existing TCP connection.

Whichever interface is used, if the destination address is in the 169.254/16 prefix, excluding the address 169.254.255.255 which is the broadcast address for the link-local prefix, then the sender must ARP for the destination address and then send its packet directly to the destination on the same physical link. This must be done whether the interface is configured with a link-local or a routable IPv4 address. In many network stacks this may be as simple as adding a routing table entry indicating that 169.254/16 is directly reachable on the local link, but that approach will not work for routers or multi-homed hosts. The host must not send a packet with a link-local destination address to any router for forwarding.

If the destination address is a unicast address outside the 169.254/16 prefix, the host should use an appropriate routable IPv4 source address if it can. If for any reason the host chooses to send the packet with a link-local source address, for example because no routable address is available on the selected interface, then it must ARP for the destination address and then send its packet directly to its destination on the same physical link, and must not send the packet to any router for forwarding. In the case of a device with a single interface and only a link-local IPv4 address, this requirement can be paraphrased as ARP for everything.

A sensible default for applications sending from a link-local address is to set the IPv4 TTL to 1, although some applications may require other values. An IPv4 packet whose source or destination address is in the 169.254/16 prefix must not be sent to any router for forwarding, and any network device receiving such a packet must not forward it, regardless of the TTL in the IPv4 header. Similarly, a router or other host must not indiscriminately answer all ARP Requests for addresses in the 169.254/16 prefix, although a router may of course answer ARP Requests for link-local addresses that it has legitimately claimed for its own use.

This restriction also applies to multicast packets: IPv4 packets with a link-local source address must not be forwarded outside the local link even if they have a multicast destination address. The non-forwarding rule means that hosts may assume that all 169.254/16 destination addresses are on-link and directly reachable. The 169.254/16 address prefix must not be subnetted. The specification uses ARP-based address conflict detection, which works by broadcasting on the local subnet, and since such broadcasts are not forwarded, allowing subnetting would let conflicts go undetected. This does not mean that link-local devices are forbidden from any communication outside the local link; hosts that implement both link-local and conventional routable IPv4 addresses may still use their routable addresses without restriction.
sections.plainLanguage:
Traffic to a link-local address never goes to a router. It is always resolved on the local wire with ARP and delivered straight to the machine that owns it.

The same rule applies to traffic leaving with a link-local source address: it must go straight to the destination rather than to a router for forwarding.

sections.title: Multiple Interfaces and Joined Networks
sections.content:
The considerations in this section also apply whenever a host has multiple IP addresses, whether or not it has multiple physical interfaces. Other examples of multiple interfaces include different logical endpoints such as tunnels and virtual private networks, and multiple logical networks on the same physical medium. This is often referred to as multi-homing. Hosts with more than one active interface that implement dynamic configuration of link-local addresses face several problems. The section lists those problems and indicates how one might solve them, but at the time of writing there is no general solution, and implementers must think the issues through before implementing the protocol on a system that may have more than one active interface.

The first problem is scoped addresses. A host may be attached to more than one network at the same time, and addresses used in one network cannot be used in another and have the same effect. Most software using TCP/IP receives messages from any interface at a particular port number and is only aware that it received a message. The first scoped address problem is source address selection: a multi-homed host has more than one address, and which one should be used as the source when sending to a particular destination is usually answered by referring to a routing table, which may not yield a good answer when the destination's range is ambiguous. The second problem is scoped parameters leaking outside their scope.

The second core problem is address ambiguity. What should a host do when it needs to send to a link-local destination that can be resolved by ARP on more than one link? Even if the address can be resolved on only one link at a given moment, there is no guarantee it will remain unambiguous, since additional hosts on other interfaces may claim it as well. Existing application software written for the IPv4 protocol suite is largely incapable of dealing with address ambiguity. Since the IP stack must have the outbound interface associated with a packet, interface selection must occur, and it cannot be derived from the packet's header parameters, so outbound interface association must be done explicitly by other means, which the specification does not stipulate.

One solution to the reachability problem is for a host to attempt to reach any host locally, using ARP, for which it receives an unreachable ICMP error message, trying all its attached links in a round robin fashion. The specification does not provide a standard solution and does not preclude implementers from supporting multi-homed configurations.

Care must be taken if a multi-homed host can support more than one interface on the same link. If those interfaces attempt to allocate the same address, they will defend the host against itself, causing the claiming algorithm to fail. The simplest solution is to run the algorithm independently on each interface configured with link-local addresses. ARP packets which appear to claim an address assigned to a specific interface indicate a conflict only if they are received on that interface and their hardware address belongs to some other interface. If a host has two interfaces on the same link, claiming and defending on those interfaces must ensure that they end up with different addresses, just as if they were on different hosts.

Hosts on disjoint network links may configure the same link-local address. If these links are later joined or bridged together, there may be two hosts on the same link trying to use the same address. When either host attempts to communicate with any other host on the network, it will at some point broadcast an ARP packet that lets the hosts detect the conflict. The resulting forced reconfiguration may be disruptive and cause TCP connections to be broken, but such disruptions are expected to be rare, and 65024 addresses are available, so even when two small networks are joined the chance of conflict for any given host is fairly small. Sending ARP replies with link-local sender addresses via broadcast instead of unicast ensures that these conflicts are detected as soon as they become potential problems. Sending periodic gratuitous ARPs in an attempt to detect the conflicts sooner is not necessary, wastes network bandwidth, and may actually be detrimental, so hosts should not send periodic gratuitous ARPs.
sections.plainLanguage:
A host on more than one network has two awkward problems. It does not know which of its addresses to use as the source, and the same link-local address may exist on two different links at once, so it cannot tell which machine it is talking to.

Two separate networks that are later joined are another awkward case: two hosts may have picked the same address, and the only way they find out is when somebody sends an ARP packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of IPv4 link-local addresses may open a network host to new attacks. In particular, a host that previously had no IP address and no IP stack running was not susceptible to IP-based attacks. By configuring a working address, the host may now be vulnerable to them.

The ARP protocol is insecure. A malicious host may send fraudulent ARP packets on the network, interfering with the correct operation of other hosts. For example, it is easy for a host to answer all ARP requests with replies giving its own hardware address, thereby claiming ownership of every address on the network. There are certain kinds of local links, such as wireless LANs, that provide no physical security, and because of the existence of such links it would be very unwise for an implementer to assume that a device communicating only on the local link can dispense with normal security precautions.

A host implementing link-local configuration has an additional vulnerability to selective reconfiguration and disruption. It is possible for an on-link attacker to issue ARP packets that would cause a host to break all its connections by switching to a new address. The attacker could force the host to select certain addresses, or prevent it from ever completing address selection. This is a distinct threat from the one posed by spoofed ARPs. Implementers and users should also note that a node that gives up an address and reconfigures allows the possibility that another node can easily and successfully hijack existing TCP connections.

Implementers are advised that the Internet Protocol architecture expects every networked device or host to implement security which is adequate to protect the resources to which it has access, including the network itself, against known or credible threats. Even though the use of link-local addresses may reduce the number of threats to which a device is exposed, implementers must not assume that a customer's local network is free from security risks. It would be misleading to make a general statement to the effect that the requirement to provide security is reduced for devices using link-local addresses as a sole means of access.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving a device an address also gives it an attack surface it did not have before, and the address resolution protocol underneath is not secure. A machine on the same wire can claim any address, and it can also push a legitimate host into changing its address and dropping its connections.

  target IP address  = the address being claimed

items.title: A new attack surface
items.text: A host that previously had no IP address and no IP stack was not exposed to IP-based attacks.

items.title: ARP has no security
items.text: A malicious host can answer all ARP requests with its own hardware address and claim every address on the network.

items.title: Wireless links are open
items.text: Some local links, such as wireless LANs, provide no physical security, so normal precautions still apply.

items.title: Forced reconfiguration
items.text: An on-link attacker can push a host into changing address, breaking its connections, or stop it from ever choosing one.

items.title: Hijacking after a change
items.text: A node that gives up an address and reconfigures lets another node take over its existing TCP connections.
